title: Im starting to feel ai game dev for amateurs is a trap
author: BloodMossHunter
selftext:
You are spending a lot of time, but will you actually ship? Will someone pay for it when better versions than you can make are already out?

I get you can make something new. But people hop to new project instead of grinding through boringly finishing the bugs in the last one and then ??? how to sell it without having visibility. 

Im just saying i thought my game would be finished after a week of buying max sub on claude. Instead i made 3 other games all in various stages of development..

This is where making a software or some tool would actually be better cause it has an end goal. A game like a book can be iterated forever. Btw when i wrote books the rule for finishers was to see a book as a project not as your baby and to actually put it out. But we didnt have crazy 2000 a day new books made w ai like it is now. Im curious if ppl without following even get visibility on itch

replies.author: Niket_N1ghtWing
replies.body: Meaning playing on their strengths, like if I am an experience gameplay programmer, i can plan out features mich better and incrementally build the game and test is along the way much better than a person who has never built anything themselves. I can do some quick changes myself not relying on prompting for everything but then I can use ai assets because that is not my strong suite. I am personally using ai very subtly only to accelerate while still holding 100% creativity and ownership of the art. I draw sketches by hand because I like to have my assets exactly how I imagine them so then I scan them and ask ai to generate me a bpy then I do the everything on that base mesh by hand. Rest of my AI use is for critiquing my design, trouble shooting, engine related issues. This has already made me so much faster and I hopefully ship by mid next year. For the current project I am coding myself mostly because that is how I started and it is a very close to the heart passion project but the next one I'll be relying much more on agentic code.

replies.author: _Fauxpaw
replies.body:
To put it more succinctly, imagine all your life you've only been watching people run marathons (*long term game development*), but were never able to actually join them. Then someone comes along, changes the rules so that people with scooters (AI) are allowed to join marathons now.

So, you join up. You already know with your scooter, you can go farther than you ever have before! Except.. as you get started, you start to realize: there's a lot of people still showing up to run without scooters, maybe out of principle. There's people showing up with scooters that you saw running just last month. And then there's the new blood - the untested people, who don't understand that even *with* a scooter, completing a marathon is going to be gruelling work that requires consistent pacing and mental fortitude.

The scooter will, undoubtedly, make it much easier. But the people at the front seem to either be those who have experience running in a marathon, whether they are using a scooter or not. Even worse, a lot - like, a lot a lot - of the new scooter marathoners are just straight up going off course, because it felt like an easier path to take at the time.

But, hey. You're in the race now. It's not a problem to drop out of it, no one will judge you for it - it's hard. Even if you're being helped along by a scooter. Some people run in the marathon without any expectation of making it on the podium, some people run even without the expectation of crossing the dang finish line.

But the act of running (creation) is, in and of itself, rewarding. But it's also hard. So don't invest more than you're willing to give up.

replies.author: LastSpark3
replies.body:
Even minimum wage is too high an expectation. The -median- indie game dev won’t break even on the Steam listing fee plus any other incidental costs or subscriptions to tools or hardware they’re developing on. The competition is insanely intense compared to almost anything else you could be trying to do in life, with an absolutely huge number of extremely high quality games for players to spend their time and money on, coming out every month.

The only reason to do this is if you have a creative vision for something you so desperately want to exist that you can tolerate the possibility of spending thousands of hours, to not even “break even” financially, because you have that intense of a compulsion to see your vision through to the end.

comments.author: NagatoKami
comments.body: Look at it as a hobby and to learn AI use cases and automate whatever tasks you can in your normal job. You can ship but you should build it in a way to not become a lifetime maintenance. Also, the market becomes oversaturated. For example, you make an app - 20$ AI monthly sub, 100$ per year to ship on the App Store, 20$ on Google Play Store. No marketing team, so expect nothing in the first year. Costs pile up. 50-60% of single devs earn between 0-100$ from apps in the end. Rough. So, keep the 20$ AI sub, make a web app with some banner ads, put the same amount in an index fund each month and you'll be better of. Let me ask you, how many games you've played from itch.io in the last month? And to how many people you donated or payed even a single dollar?

comments.author: Emu_Fast
comments.body:
Honestly my problem is I hit token limits. Grinding through bugs... No problem.

But fixing bugs is easy in the first few days of the project. Once you get over a week in the tech debt creeps in and you have a whole markdown library for scope control and you're hitting your token limit every 20-30m

And you'll specify 20 issues and it will only solve 1-2 and forget the other ones... Even if you track tickets it won't do the work. It's just like a real dev, but you can't bribe it with cookies.

Then you decide, what the hell, I'll reimplement from scratch with same hard assets and spec derived from all our active wants + chat history summarized into a design doc.

And you get something better, but it's different. It feels different. Maybe worse in some ways, but better in your most recent pain points. 

But whoops that costs a ton of tokens too. Time to wait again!

You will probably not be quitting your day job to do this, and I would suggest do not quit your day job until you have a project that has sold a bunch.

replies.author: Ferniclestix
replies.body:
my method is direct prompting, i dont say things like make me a game with swords where the main character runs around on a boulder and the boulder does jumps in a 3d platformer fantasy game world.  or stuff like that.  
games are a fully involved thing, you present the world and the player jumps in. if your going to use generated art be sure it fits perfectly with where its at. if your using text to speech be very careful that it sounds good and not fake.

as for prompting and stuff I painstakingly build out features, we need this thing here or that thing there and this needs t o be this way and that needs to respect our mouse click rules elsewhere.

https://i.redd.it/xzbsvjxtxx1i1.gif

this is what I did this morning, built a skeletal animation system for my pixel animation studio. it took me around 3 hours, ive still got some interface glitchyness, ive got to prompt a weight painting thing so i can more easily tune how the bones affect the graphic and I also have to hunt down a bug causing more and more lag each bone I add to it.   
I had to explain how exactly I want my polygon shells to warp and even had to take some screenshots of blender so claude could see what I meant about an obscure feature. (screenshots are so good in case you didnt know you can give it scribble diagrams)  
I think ive been working on this thing for 2-3 months so far.  I am almost where I aimed to be in my initial design document.  some more stuff needs adding though, some compositing things, video export and some other stuff, probably an AI model generation thing not sure.

anyway, each and every menu is prompted bit by bit, button placement everything. AI does not understand ui design. there has been many bugs along the way and ive put it down for a week at one point and was like whats the point, asperite does most of this already.

but you keep going because you have a design document a goal and maybe you wanna help people make good art or you want people to be able to have a whole bunch of fun.

Design documents are important. it helps keep you on track even if you have to take a break for a bit with your game.

comments.author: deranimusic
comments.body:
For me, AI is a tool that finally allows me to fulfill a dream I've had for the past 15 years.

I work full-time, I'm also a composer, I'm married, and I have two kids. So as you can imagine, I have very little free time to dedicate to game development. That's another reason why AI makes such a huge difference for me. It makes the whole process so much easier and allows me to make meaningful progress even with the limited time I have. I've always loved playing video games, but I've never found that one game that perfectly matches what I've always wanted.

I know quite a bit about music and can compose my own soundtracks, but when it comes to programming, I'm an absolute beginner. And that's where AI has completely changed things for me.

It's finally giving me the opportunity to slowly bring a game I've had in my head for 15 years to life, one step at a time. I also know a little bit about graphic design, but I'm incredibly grateful to be living in a time when a computer can help me accomplish something I probably would never have been able to learn on my own, even if I spent the rest of my life trying.

I actually gave game development a shot a few years ago with Godot, and failed miserably.

Now I've discovered GDevelop, and with the current version of ChatGPT, I'm making progress I honestly never thought possible. Just seeing the ideas I've carried around in my head for so many years slowly become reality is incredibly rewarding. I'm enjoying the development process itself so much that I genuinely want to keep working on my project.

If it eventually makes me a few bucks, that's great. If it doesn't, I'll still have created my very own dream game. And honestly, that's already a huge achievement for me.

I think that's one of the biggest advantages of AI right now. If your goal isn't necessarily to make a living from game development, but simply to create something you've always dreamed of, AI can open doors that would otherwise have remained closed forever.

comments.author: FoodTimely8137
comments.body:
This hits the nail on the head. The sheer velocity that AI tools give you can easily become a trap—instead of finishing one project, you suddenly find yourself juggling three half-baked prototypes because it's so easy to spin up new ideas.
​Treating a project like a finished product rather than an endless iteration cycle is tough, especially when feature creep is just a prompt away. Shipping something small, dealing with the unglamorous bug-fixing grind, and actually hitting release is a whole different discipline than just generating code.

comments.author: teapot_RGB_color

This is me prior to AI, I have accumulated an unhealthy amount of prototypes and mechanical tests in the past 20 years.

It is quite difficult to commit to the 4 digit number of hours you'll need to complete a game. You might think you'll only need hundreds of hours, but it is not reality.

You want to make sure those hours count, and there is return on investment with a game that is actually enjoyable.

I think the barrier here, that will let you commit, like really commit, is to sit down and really plan out. 

AI is great here as a sparring partner, I mean it's stupid, but it will suggest a lot of things you do not want, which force you to think things through.

comments.author: velocimposter
comments.body: 100%  So many people are seeing AI as their "way in" to game development because of it's ease of use.  They don't realizing gamedev is a complex job that requires a lot of specialized knowledge and multiple separate skill sets.  Unless you have zero expectations of players or money, then making a game is going to require dedication and learning.  A week is literally nothing, indie devs regularly take years of time to even release a game.

replies.author: ForgetoStudio
replies.body: Just choosing which game engine to use can take up to three months that is, if you want to make a good game and truly learn. Then, learning to use the tools within that engine whether it’s Unity, Unreal, or Godot, can take another three months, just to understand what every menu, button, and slider actually does... XD. And if you take the path I did and choose Three.js, you have to build the tools yourself, bit by bit. Just imagine the effort required to first create them, and then refine the specific element for which you built the tool in the first place. I’ve developed tools for things like terrain generation, vegetation refinement, biome diversity, asset placement and scaling, calibrating weapon positions based on animations, VFX, UI panels, and much more. Honestly, though, I’d recommend this approach to anyone just starting out in game development, because as you build, you’re also learning.

comments.author: Ok-Interview-8478
comments.body:
This is the trap with AI in general. It's so easy that ANYONE can do it. So people don't develop the skills or the dedication or the correct mindset to pull off a big project. The AI companies sold you a lie. They told you that buying a hammer makes you a carpenter and your house will build itself if you just "buy sub max on claude for a week."

But AI is just a tool, like a hammer. Unlike a hammer, this new tool WILL swing itself. But it won't give you passion, or discipline, or vision, or interesting ideas. You still have to develop those yourself.

EDIT: Notice I didn't saying anything about monetization above. That comes WAYYYY later. Why would anyone be interested in a game if you aren't interested in making them? We can tell if you're passionate about your project or not. Focus on falling in love with it first. Make something, ANYTHING, finished. Make it for yourself. Play it. Have your friends play it. Are you having fun? Are they having fun? Now make another one.

comments.author: nadishuddhi
comments.body:
This is true whether you use AI or not. Pretty much every project has a "mucky middle" where the work is just not very fun. The passion has worn off and the project has grown and a bunch of bugs have cropped up that you need to squash, etc. but if you believe in the project, you can finish it and at least be proud of your follow-through.

Some people make "shipping" the goal. For me, a good game is the goal. And good games take time, whether you use AI or not.
